summary: Warns Tenex users about a bug in the Tenex FTP: some Tenex programs mark the end of a line with an ASCII Unit Separator, and the FTP user program sent that over the network instead of converting it to carriage return and line feed. Non-Tenex recipients would get garbled line spacing.

eli5.summary: One kind of computer ended lines in an unusual way and forgot to fix it before sending. The other computers got messy text, so users were warned.

questions: why did tenex ftp files look wrong
subtitle: A warning about line ending problems in Tenex.

tldr.problem: Tenex programs mark line endings with ASCII Unit Separator characters, but the Tenex FTP implementation sent them over the network without conversion, breaking text on non-Tenex systems.
tldr.mechanism: FTP protocol requires line endings to be sent as carriage return and line feed pairs, regardless of how the local system marks them.
tldr.outcome: Recipients on non-Tenex systems received files with corrupted line spacing. Users were advised to convert files through TECO before sending them.

facts.label: Line ending character used by Tenex
Required protocol line ending
facts.value: Carriage Return and Line Feed (CR LF)

today: RFC 571 is a historical notice documenting an implementation issue in early Tenex FTP. It is not a specification or standard.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content: Tenex systems use an ASCII Unit Separator character to mark the end of lines in some files, instead of the standard carriage return and line feed. When users sent these files over FTP to non-Tenex computers, the FTP program did not translate these characters to the protocol-required carriage return and line feed pairs. Non-Tenex recipients would receive the files with no proper line breaks, making them unreadable or scrambled.
sections.eli5: Tenex computers use a special character that other computers don't understand to end lines. When Tenex sent files through the network, it forgot to translate that character to what everyone else uses.

sections.title: How It Affects File Transfer
sections.content: When a Tenex file containing Unit Separator line endings is sent to a receiving system like CCN, the receiver treats the entire file as a very long logical record since it does not recognize the Unit Separators. On systems like the IBM 360, the file gets folded into successive records with incorrect groupings, destroying the file's structure.
sections.eli5: The receiving computer thinks the entire file is one super-long line because it doesn't see where the lines should break.

sections.title: The Workaround
sections.content: Users can convert the file before sending it. The TECO editor, when used to load and save a Tenex file, automatically replaces all Unit Separator characters with proper carriage return and line feed sequences. Other Tenex programs that perform similar translation may also work for this purpose.
sections.eli5: Loading the file into an editor and saving it again fixes the line ending problem.
